chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who testified to the testimony of another man, so the man came and said, 'I did not testify him,' he said, 'The testimony of the more just of the two is accepted, and if the more just of the two were one, his testimony would not be accepted.'

key_terms.أَعْدَلِهِمَا: The more just of the two

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on testimony when one party denies being called as a witness?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the mechanism of *Tahkim* (arbitration) in cases of conflicting testimonies, establishing that the court accepts the testimony of the party deemed more just (*A'dal*). This principle underscores the Shia jurisprudential reliance on the moral integrity (*'Adalah*) of witnesses to resolve evidentiary disputes, distinguishing it from mere numerical majority. The ruling implies that a single witness, regardless of their justice, is insufficient for full legal proof (*Bayyinah*) in most civil matters, requiring either two witnesses or a combination of testimony and oath.
